oni.desc: The Oceanic Niño Index — 3-month running mean of Niño 3.4 SST anomalies, the official ENSO yardstick. +0.5°C sustained = El Niño; +2.0°C = very strong.
oni.inference: The ONI (3-month mean) reached +2.03°C for JJA 2026 — across the +2.0°C very-strong line months before the seasonal peak — on a trajectory now clearly steeper than 1997 or 2015 at the equivalent stage. Because it is a 3-month mean it lags the weekly Niño 3.4 (which hit +3.0°C on September 16), so the official index will keep climbing into the autumn–winter peak. The 2023-style peak-and-fade the spring flagged as the downside is long gone; this is a sustained, intensifying, potentially record event.

roni.desc: The Relative ONI strips out the tropical ocean's background warming. CPC now frames the historic-event threshold in RONI terms: ≥+2.5°C on the 3-month RONI would exceed any event since 1950.
roni.inference: RONI is the index that settles the record question, and CPC has defined it precisely: a 75% chance the 3-month RONI reaches ≥+2.5°C during Oct–Dec, which would exceed every El Niño back to 1950. The relative index is now running at or above the traditional ONI — unusual, and a sign of how strong the Niño signal is relative to the already-warm baseline. Both indices are climbing steeply together; neither argues for a weaker peak. The only open question is how far above +2.5°C RONI the event reaches.

nino34.desc: Niño 3.4 SST anomaly. The August monthly value was +2.52°C; the weekly index centred on September 16 reached +3.0°C. Eastern-basin Niño-1+2 has held above +4°C for six weeks; Niño-4 fell to +0.1°C.
nino34.inference: The monthly Niño 3.4 jumped to +2.52°C in August (from +1.4°C in July) and the weekly reading hit +3.0°C by mid-September — an extraordinary climb. The structure is strongly east-weighted: Niño-1+2 has held above +4°C for six weeks (extraordinary South-American-coast warmth) while Niño-4 fell to +0.1°C, a signature of the most intense, east-based events. IRI notes many plume models project Niño 3.4 above +3.0°C at the SON–DJF peak, beyond their highest defined category — which is why the historic-event question is now the central one.

subsurface.desc: Warm Water Volume anomaly — the subsurface heat reservoir fuelling surface warming. IRI (Sep 21): 50–150m temperatures 150°W–80°W exceed climatology by >8°C; CPC cites anomalies above +10°C at depth.
subsurface.inference: The subsurface reservoir remains exceptionally deep and continues to feed the surface. IRI reports subsurface temperatures at 50–150m between 150°W and 80°W exceeding climatology by more than 8°C, with CPC citing anomalies above +10°C at depth and a deeper-than-average thermocline. Warm east, cooler west — a major redistribution of subsurface heat that provides the energy for further surface warming through fall and winter. None of this heat has been discharged prematurely, so the reservoir still supports a climb toward a record peak.

atmosphere.desc: The Southern Oscillation Index and low-level winds confirm coupling. The SOI reached −14.6 in August and −20.1 on the latest 30-day value (through Sep 16); the Equatorial SOI was −2.5 in August.
atmosphere.inference: Ocean–atmosphere coupling is firmly established and IRI describes the evidence as compelling. The SOI was −14.6 in August and −20.1 on the latest 30-day value, with the Equatorial SOI at −2.5 — a pronounced weakening of the Walker circulation. Enhanced convection spans the Pacific from the Date Line eastward while suppression persists over Indonesia and the Philippines; low-level westerlies extend across the western-to-east-central Pacific. This is a mature, self-reinforcing Bjerknes feedback that removes any possibility of a decoupling now.

regime.name: ENSO Regime Score
regime.interp: Very strong and approaching historic. CPC: >90% very strong; 75% chance of exceeding any event since 1950 on RONI.

coupling.name: Atmospheric Coupling
coupling.interp: Firmly established. SOI near −20, Equatorial SOI −2.5, Walker circulation markedly weakened; IRI calls the coupling evidence compelling.
